podcast.title: "King of Western Swing" Title
podcast.body: Bob Wills' band quickly became the most popular act in the Western Swing genre, earning him the widespread moniker "King of Western Swing." His music blended elements from country, blues, jazz, and other styles to achieve broad appeal. "Will's band quickly became the most popular band in the genre, and he became widely known as the King of Western Swing."

podcast.title: Accusation of Plagiarism
podcast.body: While generally fostering mutual influence, Bob Wills' band was involved in at least one instance of outright stealing a Black musician's song, crediting it to a White musician, and turning it into a massive hit, which is described as "just wrong." "And suddenly that happened with Bob Willes's band at least once."

podcast.title: Creative Tension with Milton Brown
podcast.body: In the original lineup of the Light Crust Doughboys, Wills experienced a creative tension with singer Milton Brown. Brown sought to experiment more with jazz styles, while Wills preferred a traditional hill-billy string band sound, a dynamic that ultimately led to the creation of a new form of music. "Milton Brown, by all accounts, wanted to experiment more with the jazz style, while Bob Will's wanted to stick with a more traditional hill-billy string band sound."

podcast.title: Early Blackface Performances
podcast.body: Bob Wills initially performed as a blackface comedian, a practice that was very common in the US in the 1930s and even in the UK for decades longer. He later gained renown as a fiddle player and singer. "Will's originally performed as a blackface comedian."

podcast.title: Fired by W. Lee "Pappy" O'Daniel
podcast.body: In 1933, Bob Wills was fired from the Light Crust Doughboys by manager W. Lee "Pappy" O'Daniel. This was partly due to a disagreement over Wills' desire to include his brother in the band, and partly because Wills' increasing drinking habits were affecting his professionalism. podcast.title: King of Western Swing
podcast.body: Bob Wills was sometimes called the "King of Swing" by some, but he primarily billed himself as the "King of Western Swing." "A few people called Bob Will's The King of Swing too, though he mostly built himself as the King of Western Swing."

podcast.title: Mutual Respect with Les Paul and Charlie Christian
podcast.body: Bob Wills was admired by and admired musicians across racial boundaries. In 1938, jazz guitarist Les Paul traveled from Wisconsin to Tulsa, Oklahoma, specifically to hear Wills' band play, eventually jamming on stage and introducing Charlie Christian to Paul during an interval, in what was likely a rare integrated audience. "He was someone who had the respect of his peers, and he was part of a chain of influences crossing racial and stylistic boundaries."

podcast.title: Western Swing Pioneer
podcast.body: Bob Wills was one of the two biggest names in western swing, originating from Texas and later moving to Oklahoma. His style of western swing was influential, and a "paired down version" was performed by Hank Thompson. Wanda Jackson's father was a fan of his music.
